summary: Children's Nebraska, a pediatric hospital in Omaha, runs a first-of-its-kind program called Caring Contacts that sends handwritten, personalized notes from social workers to teen suicide survivors for a year after discharge. The program began May 1, 2020, and about 98% of families join. Hospital staff report that only 7% of enrolled patients return for a subsequent attempt, versus a national figure of about 27%, and they credit the low-tech, trusting contact with the results.
one_line: Children's Nebraska's Caring Contacts program sends handwritten follow-up notes to teen suicide survivors for a year, with early results showing fewer repeat attempts.
key_facts: Caring Contacts at Children's Nebraska in Omaha sends handwritten, personalized notes from hospital social work staff to teens after discharge following a suicide-related emergency visit.
Notes are sent one month, two months, three months, six months, nine months and one year after discharge, and former patients can write back.
The program was inspired by a similar program for adult suicide survivors; Sabrina Schalley pitched it to emergency department social workers in fall 2019.
Caring Contacts was set to begin on May 1, 2020, just before COVID-19 began affecting children's mental health.
Patients ages 11 and older at Children's Nebraska screen at risk of depression and/or suicide at nearly 30%.
About 98% of families offered the program agree to join, and parents or legal guardians sign a release form allowing contact for a year.

Nationally, about 27% of suicide survivors make another attempt, while 7% of enrolled Caring Contacts patients were seen in a health care setting for a subsequent attempt over the program's first three years.
Nationally, 31% to 55% of pediatric patients taken to the emergency department for a suicide attempt receive follow-up within 30 days, while 100% of Caring Contacts enrollees receive follow-up.
Before the program, teens who attempted suicide received no further contact from Children's Nebraska after discharge from the emergency department.

Schalley says most kids who attempt suicide go from thought to action in 10 minutes or less, and patients report hanging cards in rooms, keeping them in cars or backpacks, or reading them aloud to friends or family.
To Schalley's knowledge, Children's Nebraska is the first pediatric emergency department to implement such a program, and it has created a replication kit for other hospitals and organizations.
Social workers Mackenzie Parks and Eva Doescher said the program helps families know staff truly care and helps staff hear how youth are progressing.
